title: Smallies v. Biggies
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart introduces a two-tier framework for explicitly teaching classroom behaviors, building on the concept he calls Woodenization after basketball coach John Wooden's famous first lesson on tying shoes. Smallies are quick habits students can master in a single five-minute lesson, like how to enter the room or format notes, but they require ongoing reinforcement rather than reteaching when they lapse. Biggies are complex skills, like note-taking or essay writing, that must be taught repeatedly through modeling and feedback because they take much longer to develop. His central claim is that misidentifying which tier a behavior belongs to wastes teacher effort, since Smallies fail when treated as one-and-done and Biggies fail when treated as something a single mini-lesson can fix.
points: Stuart's Smallie/Biggie distinction gives teachers a diagnostic question for any classroom routine: is a lapse a reinforcement problem or a skill-development problem, because the fix for each is different.
His scripted response to a Smallie lapse (pull aside, ask why, remind of technique, offer help, no shame, no letting it slide) models firm-but-warm reinforcement rather than reteaching or punishment.
The framework reframes consistent reinforcement as the actual lever for Smallies, since the five-minute mini-lesson itself was never the hard part.
quotes: The most powerful thing you can do to improve student effort is teach them, very clearly and well, what good effort looks like.

Smallies are things that you can reasonably expect your students to comprehend within five minutes or so of direct instruction. Typically, then, these are things they've been taught many times before.

This is the critical and inevitable moment with the Smallie. In this situation, it's not that the student doesn't know how to tie his shoes like John Wooden taught him to. It's that the player forgot, or the player was distracted, or the player was in a hurry.

This is what I imagine John Wooden did: pull the player aside, ask him why his shoe came untied, remind him of the proper technique and why it's important, ask him if he needs anything to help him be successful in this area moving forward.
Biggies, on the other hand, are behaviors that you'll need to teach through modeling, examples, non-examples, and so on, many times in order for your students to grow to understand them.
Whereas Smallies are mostly matters of habit, Biggies are mostly matters of skill. And so Biggies, of course, must be taught many, many times.
